title: Notes of Ministry - 92 - July 1980

source.file: Various/Notes of Ministry - 92 - July 1980 (2497)/Notes of Ministry - 92 - July 1 - Various.epub

paragraphs.text: It sometimes is said in christian circles, ‘Well, what can one person do in the circumstances?’
As believers, those who have part in God’s testimony, the primary answer to the question is,

‘What has one Man not done?’—“I have glorified thee on the earth, I have completed the work which thou gavest me that I should do it”, John 17: 4. That one Man is Jesus, as we know. Totally abandoned by His lovers and associates, left entirely alone in accomplishing the work in which God was glorified, He glorified God “on the earth”. As another has said, it would not have been morally right for Him to have died on the earth, because He glorified God on it; but He was lifted up between earth and heaven and died on the cross. In Jesus we have perfectly what one Man has done, and He did it alone. That is really the answer to the question. If men ask such things, and they do so frequently, you can always speak to them about the Lord Jesus; tell them what one Man has done. You can tell them what He has done for God, and you can tell them what He has done for them, and what He has done for you. If you speak of what He has done for you, you speak from experience, but you can say the answer is in what one Man has done for God. In the light of what the Lord Jesus has done, let us not, dear brethren, ever ask, ‘What can one man, or one person, do?’
But I wanted to extend this with a word of exhortation for all of us. The Lord Jesus, of

course, stands alone in all His perfection, absolutely and infinitely perfect. But there are many examples in Scripture of persons of like passions to ourselves standing alone, and we find examples of what one person can do in the ways of God, doing it, of course, with the support of God. So I selected these three scriptures which I hope may encourage us. The first is about Epaphras. Here we have a man who was earlier called “a faithful minister” (Colossians l: 7).
He is not called that here, he is called “one of you”. Jesus elsewhere speaks of “two of you”.

This is not two of you, it is one of you. Epaphras, I think, is demonstrating to us what one man of like passions with ourselves can do in connection with the beloved people of God, in order to help them, having before him that they should stand perfect and complete in all the will of God. So Paul says, “always combating earnestly for you in prayers”—a plural word—

“to the end that ye may stand perfect and complete in all the will of God”. This is not something that is out of the range of any one of us; it requires perseverance, that is pretty evident; but it is not out of the range of any brother or sister, alone, to engage in this wonderful service of combating earnestly for the saints, the local saints.

He was “one of you”, a local brother. We could extend it to a local sister, too, concerned that the saints should be getting on, growing in the true knowledge of God, and growing by the true knowledge of God, the person that is combating having nothing less before him than what God has before Him, that the saints should stand perfect and complete in all the will of God. I believe, dear brethren, if we took up this simple practice more, and committed ourselves to it, we should find the truth being made effective in the saints, and positive progress being made amongst them towards

the great end that God has before Him, that they should enter into His purpose. For my part I feel how little I engage in it. Perhaps I could say I pray a little more than I used to, because I have a little more time, but I am concerned about the question of engaging in combat for the saints, which is not simply prayer. It is, I believe, becoming engaged in prayers in the power of the Spirit against the enemy, so it is called combat.

I would like to ask each one of us here, especially the older brothers and sisters, What do you know about this? I ask myself, What do I know about it? We have a small company in Gillingham; one thinks of that company as precious to Christ. I think of the objective that the Lord has before Him in connection with that company. You cannot necessarily pray this prayer, or combat in this way for every company. I do not know, if Epaphras had been local in Corinth, what he would have prayed for them, or what he would combat for them, but his main objective would be the same, because God has in mind that all the saints should come into the knowledge and enjoyment of His purpose; but I suppose the combat would relate to the present state of the saints in any locality. I would desire to encourage us all to look at this passage and seek to take it up with God, but I can assure you that it will require perseverance.

The enemy is set against God’s people coming into His purpose for them. The conflict is between God and Satan, and man’s soul is the battleground. I would be more concerned for myself and for my brethren that we might enter into this combat, that Satan’s foothold among the saints might be removed, so that they might move forward progressively towards this great end to which I have referred.
Now Epaphras had this in mind; he was not just a faithful minister. There were two prophets,

Haggai and Zechariah, and it says of them that they prophesied and that they helped the people (see Ezra 5: 1, 2). They did not only prophesy but they helped the people. I think, dear brethren, it is not sufficient simply to prophesy; it is not sufficient to teach, or to have the scope of the truth before us, but we need to have simple confidence in God, to persevere in combat, because the enemy is set to dislodge Christ from the place that He has in the affections of the saints, and to hinder them from progress in the knowledge of God. There is a word in the Old Testament, “And he said, For the hand is on the throne of Jah; Jehovah will have war with Amalek from generation to generation”, Exodus 17: 16. It means, I believe, in its application, that the effort of the enemy in the activity of his hand is to dislodge Christ from having complete sway over His people as in the testimony of our Lord. No doubt his objective would be to remove God from His position, to rob Him of His rights in every area, be it in the government of the world, in the assembly, in our localities, or in individuals. He would try if he can to break the moral sway of God in the souls of His people. And that is going on all the time—from generation to generation—because the flesh does not change. So, dear brethren, we are up against one who has often been called a very wily foe, but, thank God, greater is He that is in us than he that is in the world. The One that is in us, the Holy Spirit, gives us power to enter into this combat for the saints.

Now in particular, I think, it refers to our localities. Sometimes we think that numbers indicate moral strength and fibre, but that is far from the truth. A few in a locality may have moral fibre, and may be in the power of the present testimony of God. A large number may be out of it. I think that would be fairly obvious to all of us.

Our desire should be to be so with God that whether we be few or many we might be marked by moral power and giving place to Christ in our souls, and that each in his locality should be marked by this combat, that the saints might stand perfect and complete in all the will of God.

Now you may say, Is it possible that every one in every locality would do that? I would say, You do it; You pray; You take it up. You may be one of two in a locality. It only says, “one of you” without saying of how many; you may be one of two, or one of two hundred; I would say, You take it up. You may say, We have many others in the locality who share the responsibility; that may be true, but I would say to each of us here, however many or few you may be in your locality, You take it up. God will honour it. You will learn from practical experience what one person can do, how one person can be effective in the maintenance of what is due to God, and in contributing to the progress of his local brethren in the knowledge of God. So you be one—one like Epaphras—“one of you”.

We are thankful to have “two of you” which stands in a similar connection—“Whatsoever it may be that they shall ask it shall come to them from my Father who is in the heavens. For where two or three are gathered together unto my name, there am I in the midst of them”, Matthew 18: 19, 20. But I thought it would be interesting and more encouraging to us in this meeting if I referred to “one of you”. Now you be the one; you be an Epaphras in your locality. You may say, I have heard that said before. Yes, I have too; I would desire to be exercised myself, and to exercise you personally in your locality to be an Epaphras in relation to your local brethren.

Then, further than that. Epaphras laboured for the saints in Laodicea and Hierapolis. However wide the boundary of your prayers and your combat, so wide will be your influence amongst the saints; you will find that. You may pray for brethren many miles away and not contact or see them or hear from them. Well, God is not limited; if we can humbly submit our prayer, and combat with God about the saints, wherever they may be, in our locality, or beyond. God is not limited to the person who is combating to accomplish His end. You may pray for someone in a locality hundreds or thousands of miles away; God has His own means of answering that prayer—His own agency, His own vessel, or He may operate directly. He has the power to do it. I think therefore the Lord would raise the question with us as to where our faith is. You remember He says in one place, “O thou of little faith”, Matthew 14: 31. He says in another place, “Where is your faith?”, Luke 8: 25. Where is it? They were on the storm-troubled lake, and the ship nearly full of water. Jesus was in the ship but He says, “Where is your faith?” It is little, we often have to own, but ‘ Where is it?’ seems to me to be even more challenging. And I think, dear brethren, it calls for faith to take these things up. So even if I may be the only one in my locality who is an Epaphras, let me be an Epaphras; I say, whatever the conditions, You take it up.

Now the next example is Paul. We all know about Paul and how he says that at his first defence no man stood with him. So here is another man who was alone. I wonder what Paul would say if you said to him, as to your particular difficult circumstances, ‘What can one person do?’ You know what he said to Timothy, who evidently was drooping—rather like us.

Do you ever droop? I find I do. Do you ever decline in your affections? Does your zeal sometimes become weak? Well, I think Paul demonstrated in himself what one person could do. That man had confidence in the

Lord— implicit confidence. He says, “I know, whom I have believed”, that is, ‘I am conscious’—it is conscious knowledge—‘whom I have believed’, “and am persuaded”—this is one of Paul’s persuasions, he had others also—“that he is able to keep for that day the deposit I have entrusted to him”. That is to say, despite the darkening state of the assembly, the apostasy—and “all who are in Asia ... have turned away from me” (2 Timothy 1: l5)—
despite it all, he was persuaded that the Lord was able to carry him through. That strengthened the man to stand alone. He says, “The Lord stood with me”, 2 Timothy 4: 17.
He was not quite like Jesus, because there was a time when Jesus had no one with Him. Paul was never entirely alone, never, because he says, “The Lord stood with me”, and he had
.implicit confidence in the Lord Jesus.

Now that is another matter I would like to stimulate amongst us, confidence in the. Lord Jesus. We said in our reading that it is the testimony of our Lord. Paul is indicating, I believe, that he is fully convinced in his confidence in the Lord that He will see that testimony through to its full consummation in glory. This confidence is seen in one man, Paul. Now he virtually says to Timothy, ‘You be a man, Timothy’. He is speaking to an individual, one man. He is telling Timothy, putting it simply, what one man can do, a man who was not very strong and had frequent illnesses. Evidently he had stomach illnesses of some kind. Paul says to him, “Drink no longer only water, but use a little wine on account of thy stomach and thy frequent illnesses”, 1 Timothy 5: 23. He might make many an excuse, as we do, plead his weaknesses, and so on, but Paul would encourage him to “be strong in the grace which is in Christ Jesus”, 2 Timothy 2: 1. I think the Lord would encourage our younger brethren in this way; if it is only one man—like Timothy—we would encourage him to be strong in the

grace which is in Christ Jesus. What grace that is! I think it is experienced as we abide in Him. It is not something which is communicated, so to speak, a lot at a time, but you experience the inward strength as you abide in Him.

Remember, as I have already said, that Paul is speaking to one man. Men of God have told us to read the Scriptures as if they were written to us personally. So this is a letter, so to speak, from Paul to me! Read it as if it is written to you. When Paul speaks of Timothy as his true child and the like, we would never put ourselves in the same category, but what Paul exhorts Timothy to do I would read as though it were written to me. Can you do that? Now I do not believe that Timothy, in any sense, worshipped Paul, or allowed Paul to come between him and God, so that when Paul departed Timothy’s faith stood in the power of God. What he received from Paul he would give thanks for; he knew about him, his manner of life, his conduct, his purpose, his teaching, and so on, but Timothy had his own link with God, and the truth was made good in the soul of that man so that, according to profane history, he himself was martyred.

When Paul went, everything did not go to pieces for Timothy. When Mr. Darby died, for some people everything finished. When I was a boy we had an old man who used to come into our meeting in Strood and when we sang Mr. Darby’s hymns the tears rolled down his face. He was a dear man, but he made it plain that, as far as he was concerned, when Mr.

Darby died that was the finish. That is where he stopped. Others thought everything finished when Mr. Raven died; others think, or thought, that everything finished when Mr. Taylor died; but the continuity of everything in ministry and in the truth is in the Spirit of God. We do

need to understand that, and I am absolutely sure that as far as Timothy was concerned he would not fall into the snare of doing homage to Paul. I am equally certain that if he had done. Paul would say, “See thou do it not. I am thy fellow-bondman”, Revelation 19: 10. So Timothy would move in his own relation with God as an individual, although as an individual he would be thankful for others in the same path with whom he could walk.

I would like to make a few references to Hannah, because she was a sister. There is no reflection on our sisters implied in the fact that I have read about two brothers and only one sister, because there is ample evidence in Scripture of sisters who were alone with God and had in mind His testimony. I thought of Hannah and her bitterness of soul and her sorrow.

You think of the dark background in which she was. The lamp of God had not yet gone out, but the scripture seems to imply that it was well on the way to do so. The background was very dark. There was Eli, and we would be careful in what we say about him, but at any rate he had declined. He was sitting down, which as far as I know the priest should never have done when in function. It says he “sat upon the seat by the doorpost of the temple of Jehovah”. Hannah was in bitterness of soul. I do not think she was in bitterness of soul simply because she had not a child, but because she was thinking of God’s testimony. She was thinking of Jehovah and His interests, of His people, and the deplorable state in which they were.

Dear brethren, you think of the deplorable state publicly in which believers are, scattered far and wide. I understand there are well over 400 different groups or sects of believers in this country alone. What a deplorable condition! The condition among God’s people was deplorable at

this time. Here is an exercised woman. We would love that our sisters might also be exercised. I believe they give character and substance to our occasions. We can all be exercised to be giving even more body and substance. You may say, ‘What can one woman do?’ Well, what did Hannah do? There is no record that she ever saw the full result of what God did in answer to her prayers, in Samuel becoming the great link, the prophetic link, between God and His people; but her exercises were before God. The official priesthood thought she was drunk; the Lord’s own brethren thought He was mad. Eli says to her, “Put away thy wine from thee”. She says, “I have drunk neither wine nor strong drink”. She had vowed a vow, and in our day we can make committals to the Lord and the testimony. What about your locality, dear sister? Are you in the spirit of Hannah? What is required? What was required in Israel at this time? What was required was a man—a man of God. And Hannah’s asking for a man child meant that what was in her mind was a man of God. That is what Samuel became. Think of that coming in, through God’s mercy, through the exercises of one woman in a very dark day.
Now what can one person do? What can you do, dear sister, in your locality? You may say, ‘Well, I cannot speak in the assembly’. But at any rate you can pray; you can be with God.

You can be discerning as to what is needed in your locality, and what is needed in the assembly generally. You can be exercised about it. You can be feeling, as is said of Hannah, in bitterness of soul about conditions. And then I think you will find, as you are with God, that your influence and effectiveness will extend in the locality. There will be greater substance and greater power given to the assemblings of the saints. And you may never see the full answer. You say, ‘Well, that is rather sad that

Hannah may not have seen the full answer’. Stephen never saw the conversion of Saul, did he? The last he saw of Saul was the stoners’ clothes being laid at his feet. He never lived to see what Paul became, as one of the greatest servants, if not the greatest, of the despised Jesus. And yet it was the witness of Stephen that had affected Saul’s conscience. No doubt the Lord used it, as he says to Saul, “It is hard for thee to kick against goads”, Acts 26: 14.
And we are not told whether Hannah saw Samuel in his prime, if I may use such an expression, when he was the great prophetic link between God and His people.

What I wanted to draw attention to is what one man or one woman of like passions with ourselves can do; what one person can do, so that we may never be guilty hereafter of saying in almost morbid depression, ‘Well, what can one person do?’ Let us look into the Scriptures and we shall find a multitude of instances of what one person did, because that one person was with God. May we be more with Him, dear brethren, in particular about our own localities, like Epaphras and Paul, but then extending from our own locality so that the boundary of our influence may become greater because the boundary of our prayers is wider.
May it be so for His pleasure.
God’s glad tidings present to men great

accomplished facts, things which cannot be questioned, matters which stand immutable beyond every question which men may venture to bring. We have often noticed how in this powerful address after Pentecost Peter presents the facts, but in a manner which is intended to affect every one of us. I have to ask myself, Where do I stand in reference to these great facts of which Peter is speaking? He spoke nearly twenty centuries ago, but the facts remain; they remain unchangeable, and men are brought by God’s word to see where they stand in reference to the facts.

What these remarkable passages that I have read particularly lead to is the wonderful fact of a living Man in heaven, a glorious Man, and in consequence of His exaltation the Holy Spirit come here, come into God’s house here. These are facts that remain, facts which in their bearing remain the same. Though the times, in the sense of what men do, have changed so remarkably since these words were spoken, the glorious facts remain. And I have to ask myself, What is my life in reference to that glorious Man up there and to the Holy Spirit here? Have you a link with Christ up there? Is He the absorbing object of that heart of yours?

Does He in His glory, being who He is, and if I may use the expression with reverence, being what He is up there, eclipse everything else that men might present to you? He is a heavenly Christ, a Man in heaven, One to whom God has committed everything, One who is perfectly competent to have everything according to God under His hand. He shall come into the scene from which He was rejected, spurned and crucified, in the might of power, and secure everything in perfect order according to God. What link have you here and now with that glorious Person, a living, glorified Man who has none the less His eye upon you? As you read the Scriptures and hear the word His eye is upon you. We are not

speaking of things as men speak of history, we are not speaking of things as mere information, the point is the blessed, glorious reality of a living Man being in heaven exalted into the place of pre-eminence by God, and the blessed Spirit of God, the Holy Spirit, having come.

What do these things mean to you? It is a terrible thing to be outside of them; God has no thought that you should be outside of them. We have been speaking of God’s grace, and God’s grace is surpassingly wonderful in the way it works with men, women, and young persons, but it works in connection with Christ where He is in the glory. What is He to you?

There was adequate witness as He was here, “a man borne witness to by God to you by works of power and wonders and signs, which God wrought by him in your midst, as yourselves know”. What a penetrating, powerful word! What an exposure of the world that cast Him out!

Perhaps some of us need that, a real exposure of the world that rejected Him in all its elements and aspects; what men speak of as the cultured ones as well as the morally hateful ones are features of the world that rejected Christ. It is a challenge whether we are clinging to any of the features of that world, even features which may not be grossly immoral or offensive but which none the less spring up out of the world that has rejected the Lord of glory.

“As yourselves know—him, given up by the determinate counsel and foreknowledge of God”. God was in this matter; this would baffle many of Peter’s hearers, rejecting Christ as they had done, to be assured that God was in their rejecting Him in the sense that He was to go vicariously into death. How marvellously God works; but He does not work as men away from Him might determine. He is not hindered by what the thoughts of men might

be; He is God, He is able to intervene in His own way. But why does He intervene? For blessing, to secure your heart for Christ, to secure you as knowing the blessedness of the gift of the Holy Spirit, to be in the full light of God as His glad tidings would present Him to you.

That is the thought with God. It was necessary that that glorious Person should die. Have we a true judgment of sin? Are we apt in these days in which we live to be so much affected by the course of things that surrounds us that our judgment of sin is blunted? Let us get our eye on the cross of Jesus, “ye, by the hand of lawless men, have crucified and slain”. What was seen in Jesus was a spotless life which none could call in question, a life lived under the eye of God and fragrant to Him in every detail of it. It set forth the divine ideal in man in an absolutely unqualified sense, yet such a life as this was brought to an end, as the outward appearance would support, by lawless men in crucifying Him.

I say ‘the outward appearance’ because the outward side was that lawless men placed Him on the cross to die; the other side of the matter, the divine side of the matter, is that He laid down His life. He did it, He laid down His life, and that on your account. There could be no modifying of divine judgment as to sin, and the purging of the guilt of your sins could only be by the bearing of that guilt by Jesus upon the cross, forsaken by God. There is the outward side of the matter and there is the divine side of the matter, and God would bring you into His side of the matter, what Jesus has effected for Him—and for you too, according to the riches of His grace.

Could there be anyone here who would stand alongside those who rejected Him? It was “by the hand of lawless men”, and yet the lawless men were not the sole ones who had the guilt, “him ye, by the hand of lawless men, have crucified and slain”. You might say it is the solemn, divine view of the nation of Israel as having rejected Christ, but the gentile nations came into it, as we know, and endorsed the rejection, and the world endorses it still. You may not credit that. It is something that some people find very hard to accept, an assertion that the world endorses His rejection still. Go out into Nostrand Avenue and preach Christ, and you may find one here and one there who is attracted and will say, ‘I love the Lord Jesus, He is my Saviour; I believe in the Lord Jesus Christ’. There are such, thank God, but as to the crowd that passes down Nostrand Avenue, what will you actually experience from them? They will pass on, their steps will quicken; they do not want to hear about Jesus. Their consciences may be exposed, and yet they do not want to hear about Jesus. And yet we have in mind the wonderful facts, that He went to the cross, He suffered and died there. His precious blood was shed as the soldier smote His side; the atonement was wrought in suffering and death and bloodshed by Jesus, and it is a glorious, completed matter. That is the fact; there is nothing more to be done; the one sacrifice has taken place and God has borne witness to His absolute acceptance of it. How? By raising Jesus from the dead.

I am impressed today with the need of getting a greater sense of resurrection power, the power that raised up Jesus, the power that has its bearing upon those who love Him, to set them free from the whole dominion of death in the scene out of which Christ died. Though we be in it as to our bodies and walk for a little time until He come. He would free us from the dominion of death and bring us into the glorious light of life as we know it in Him. God has raised Him, “Whom God has

raised up, having loosed the pains of death, inasmuch as it was not possible that he should be held by its power”. It was not possible that He who did no sin, neither was guile found in His mouth, He who went that way entirely vicariously (that is, on account of others and not on account of any need of His own) could be held by death. He came out of death in the might of His power. “This Jesus has God raised up, whereof all we are witnesses”. Notice how that is emphasized, the reality of the fact that God has raised Him, and that as being raised He had to do with His disciples for forty days before He went into heaven. That is, men were to be brought into the real experience of having to do with a Man raised from the dead, even Jesus, that their thoughts might be not limited to what lies on this side of death but transferred to the glory of a Man out of death. And we need to have our minds transferred from the scene of death, and what belongs to it, to a scene that is dominated by Christ, whom death cannot touch, and have Him as the contemplation of our hearts.

So he goes on, “Having therefore been exalted by the right hand of God”—exalted, given the highest place; the right hand of God is the place of power. What a time it will be when Jesus comes in power and takes up His rights in this very scene! I was impressed by that this morning as we gathered to break bread. We gather in the light of the fact that He is rejected here, and we feel His rejection and His absence, but this very scene is yet to witness the glory and power in which He shall come and display perfect competence to hold everything according to God—all in the hand of one glorious Man. What the world is looking for is a man that has the competence to hold rule and to keep peace and to prevent insurrection.
There is only one glorious Man that shall do it, and that

is Jesus. The confusion of these times politically, commercially, and socially should have its voice to all of us, a negative voice maybe, but a strong one, to turn us to Jesus as the One by whom everything shall be set in order at His coming. When you see the disorder you think of how these things will work when Christ is on the throne, when His sway is extended everywhere, when everything shall be in a moral order that has never been seen before.

Yet that same glorious Person, exalted as He is, would engage and fill your heart here and now. You do not have to wait for His public manifestation; we may have to wait for a little for that, but you do not have to wait to come into the knowledge and appreciation of the self-same glorious Person who shall come in a cloud from heaven with mighty power. He would have you to know Him tonight, to have Him to fill your heart tonight, to have Him to fill your life. All these things are great facts—His death is a fact, the shedding of His precious blood is a fact, His burial is a fact, His rising is a fact, His exaltation is a glorious fact, and you have to examine where you stand in respect of all these great facts. They are things that are immutable; men may seek to criticise and to invalidate them in their wicked arguments, but they stand as being of God.

Then Peter says, “having received of the Father the promise of the Holy Spirit, he has poured out this which ye behold and hear”; he is referring to the fact that the Holy Spirit had come; and He is still here. Do you know the Spirit? Are you conscious of having received the Spirit?

Do you find something in yourself that gives you an impression of the exceeding love of Christ, and links your heart with Himself up there? It is the Holy Spirit who delights to do that. Do you find power to reject what is not of Christ? The Holy

Spirit gives power to reject what is not of Christ. If you find difficulty, find yourself being drawn away perhaps into the elements of the world that refused Him, turn to God and seek the gift of the Holy Spirit, intensely real as it is in the sense of power. He will go with you every moment of the day. One who will witness in that heart of yours to things which are not of God, warn you against them, and give you power to turn from them. But He will always turn your heart to Jesus to find some fresh glory that you have never discerned before in that glorious Person, and give you to know the reality of life in relation to Christ in glory. That is life, real life!

The blessedness of that is, something which perhaps some of us have never yet fully touched; but the reality of a life that is lived in relation to a glorified Christ and enjoyed in the gift of the Spirit is something which God would have us brought to as we hear His word to us. It enters into the whole life of the person. How many, alas, there are who think of christianity, to use a very common expression, as a one-day-a-week matter. In fact it is to be, according to God, a continual matter, a matter of the most precious enjoyment; there is a spring of power that gives strength for a responsible walk here under the eye of God that is pleasing to Him, and that is what is in mind. May this be the issue of the bearing of these facts upon every one of us. The facts cannot be changed, but the point of God’s word to us, as it goes out in this favoured time, is where each one of us stands in reference to the glorious facts which God presents to us. May He bless His word for His name’s sake.

articles.title: “HOLDING FORTH THE WORD OF LIFE”
articles.author: E. C. Burr
articles.meeting: Word at the burial of Mrs, J. S. Pugh

paragraphs.text: These verses remain in my mind, especially since this was the part of the scripture that entered into our reading in this room last week. They remained there especially because, while I do not specifically refer to murmurings and reasonings, one characteristic for which I remember, and shall remember, our sister, is the continuous uncomplaining way in which she was amongst us. Many a time most of us who have seen her here would have thought she was quite unfit to be out, but not only had she overcome to be amongst us, but she had no complaint about her condition either. I carry this lesson myself from our sister, and I commend it to the brethren, that doing “all things without murmurings and reasonings” is a reflection of that. The word as to murmurings and reasonings is not a word to some of the brethren, it is a word to them all, and we would bear in mind that Paul is addressing the whole company. Since his letter has come down to us, he is addressing us all. Therefore his injunction as to murmurings and reasonings bears on all the brethren.

But it was not that side of the verses that I had so much in mind, although it was because of that that I was thinking about them, but the closing words that Paul uses, “holding forth the word of life”. I think that they particularly bear on us at a time when death is so markedly before us, and when, if we are sober, we have to say that death may be even more before us unless the Lord comes. I wonder sometimes whether we sufficiently

carry the degree to which death might be amongst us if the Lord does not come. None of us, of course, knows whom the Lord might take next, but we are in a scene that is characterized by death and in a condition that is characterized by death, and death is all around us. It is not so much, although it is true, that we are in a crooked and perverted generation—that describing the general moral characteristics of the day—but that we are in a scene which is characterized by death, and in that, Paul says, “holding forth the word of life”.

Now, beloved, what an injunction for us. It does not matter how old we are or how young we are, but it is “holding forth the word of life”. That is to say that in a world characterized by death, and in a condition characterized by death, we are to be here as bearing Paul’s word; we are to be here with this, not only in our minds, but in expression in us, that we are holding forth the word of life. That is to say that believers, the saints, the brethren, are to be characterized by that which is the reverse of what is around us—in a world of death we hold forth the word of life.

Now what does that mean? I suppose we could link it with chapter 1 of John’s gospel, where we have “In the beginning was the Word” (John 1: 1), “And the Word became flesh, and dwelt among us” (John 1: 14), but “In him was life, and the life was the light of men” (John 1: 4). We could say, I think without straining the scripture, that in Jesus the word of life was held forth; in fact, not only was it held forth in testimony, but it was actually conveyed to persons. When we consider the three persons that He raised from among the dead, the Word of life was there effectively in its current operation; not only in testimony—that is, not only in what was said—but something communicated, communicated, of course, by Him as the Son of God in divine power.

having power to raise the dead. It raises the question with us whether we have ourselves the power to communicate something. On this account Peter would not leave Jesus at the end of John 6; “To whom shall we go? thou hast words of life eternal”. The fact that he knew Jesus as the One in whom, I might say, the word of life and the words of life eternal were held forth was enough to retain Peter for Christ when many of His disciples went away backward.

I trust, beloved, that all of us have found the word of life in Jesus. May it be so, and may it increasingly be so. I have been somewhat concerned as to myself as to whether more is held in doctrine than is held in relation to the Person of Christ as a known Person; and the word of life is in Him. So Peter in the Acts was enjoined to go into the temple and speak “all the words of this life”, Acts 5: 20. Of course, he actually spoke, but people would see in Peter something that was characterized by what was different from the world all around him, that there was a man who was characterized by the knowledge of a life that was not to be constrained or hindered or held back by what characterized the world in which he lived.

Beloved, that is open to us, to be the expression of life. I believe that one thing the Lord would do with us in the present day is to enlarge our understanding of divine things and give us greater energy in relation to them. May this happen, beloved, and then it will be clear that the word of life is held forth. It is the answer to death; in a certain sense it is the only answer that we have to death, the holding forth the word of life, ourselves held in relation to Jesus glorified, and finding in the word of life which we hold, forth not only satisfaction for ourselves in what is permanently living, but also that we have an answer to the whole environment in which we live.

If you relate this to Numbers 17, you will find that it is actually the answer to the murmurings and reasonings. In that chapter God said, Lay up the staves one for each of the tribes of Israel, and He said, I will make the murmurings to cease. How did He make the murmurings to cease? In a certain sense, by application, He held forth life. He held forth the word of life, the staff which budded and brought forth buds and blossoms and ripened almonds; there in a sense you have the word of life held forth; it was that condition of life which was the answer to every murmuring and feeling amongst the children of Israel.

Beloved, I think that the Lord would stimulate us, even in the presence of death, that there is life. As I say, none of us knows who may be the next that the Lord takes and how much we may have to confront death if the Lord leaves us here, but in the midst of it all there is life.

And not only is there life, but there is the word of life, and that is to be held forth. We could not then fail to be a light in the world. May we be encouraged by this that in the presence of death there is the word of life and it is open to each of us, young or old, to hold it forth. Paul here says it will be a testimony to him in Christ’s day, that he has “not run in vain nor laboured in vain”. None of us is looking for that kind of return the glory will be Christ’s; but let us be sure that the word of this life is what we are holding forth in this dying scene.

articles.title: THE GLORY THAT SHALL BE REVEALED
articles.author: A. J. Gaskin

paragraphs.text: The day is shortly coming,
When Thou blest Lord shalt see
An answer to Thy travail,
When we shall with Thee be,
There, Thou in heavenly glory
Shalt be the centre blest
Of myriads changed and living
Who find in Thee their rest.
Oh what a blaze of glory
That heavenly scene shall be!
Each shining in Thy image
At rest in peace and free.
And oh what paeans of praises
Our willing tongues shall raise,
To Thee who art so worthy
Of worship, love and praise.
What blessed realisation
That glorious time will prove,
God’s wondrous sovereign counsels
Secured in endless love.
For then our eyes shall see Thee
Unhindered face to face,
Thou, blessed Lord, enjoying
The triumphs of Thy grace.
Aberdeen, April 1980
(This was composed, I understand, on the way home from the London meetings in April, when the Lord’s return was a leading impression—Ed.)
